unit.title: Diagnose and repair faults in electrical and electronic systems

summary: This unit teaches you to find and put right faults in electrical and electronic systems: installation circuits, motor control circuits, sensors and drives, and the power supplies and boards inside control equipment. You will plan a logical search, use drawings and instruments to find the fault and its root cause, repair it with the right parts, prove the repair and report to the client. At Level 3 you also lead the job and check the work of others.

blocks.p: This unit is about **systems**: the circuits, controls and electronics that make lights, pumps, conveyors, gates, alarms and drives work together. A fault in a system often shows up far from its cause. A breaker trips because of water in an outdoor sign; a pump will not start because a float switch has failed; a gate controller resets because a diode in its power supply has gone open. Your job is to trace the symptom back to the cause, repair it properly and prove the system works. (Faults inside individual pieces of equipment, such as transformers, generators, motors and power tools, are the subject of MEMMRD0443A.)

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the fault-finding job
Get the fault report, the job history, the drawings and the manuals; agree the shutdown, access and timing with the client before you start.
Work safely on systems
Isolate every source of supply, make stored energy safe, keep live testing for competent authorised people, and protect electronic parts from static.
Use a logical method
Confirm the symptom, list the likely causes, test in a planned order (half-split, input to output, most likely first) and record every reading.
Use instruments correctly
Choose the right instrument, range and category rating; read the results correctly and spot false readings.
Find faults in installation circuits
Trace trips, earth faults, loose connections, voltage problems, a lost neutral and intermittent faults.
Find faults in control circuits and drives
Follow a schematic through starters, relays, sensors and variable speed drives, and find faults in the motors they control.
Find and replace faulty electronic parts
Test power supplies, diodes, capacitors, regulators, resistors and transistors; desolder and solder to a good standard.
Repair the root cause with the right parts
Match every rating, decide between repair and replacement, and fix the real cause rather than the symptom.
Prove the repair
Carry out dead tests, then have a competent person energise and function-test the system; watch it run.
Report and lead
Write a clear fault report, explain it to the client in plain words, and brief, supervise and check junior workers.

blocks.h: Systems in Jamaica: what you will meet

ul: JPS supplies homes and most businesses at **110/220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz**, using two lines and a shared neutral. Larger buildings, hotels and factories also have three-phase supplies.

The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, so you will hear US terms (grounding, GFCI, equipment grounding conductor) and British terms (earthing, RCD, protective conductor). This kit gives both.

Many buildings have **more than one source of supply**: standby generators with automatic transfer switches, solar PV with battery inverters, and UPS units. Every one of them must be found and isolated before you work.
Much equipment is imported from the US and some of it is built for **60 Hz**. Check nameplates: equipment rated only for 60 Hz may run slow or hot on Jamaica's 50 Hz supply.
Heat, humidity and salt air near the coast corrode terminals and boards; rats and insects get into panels; lightning and storms damage electronics.

blocks.note: Many faults in Jamaica start after lightning, a storm, flooding or a power cut. Always ask the client whether the fault began after one of these. It points you towards surge damage to power supplies, boards and drives, or towards water in outdoor equipment.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: At Level 2 you followed instructions. At Level 3 you plan the fault-finding, decide the order of tests, choose the instruments, judge the readings, decide whether to repair or replace, lead a small team and write the report. You must also know when to stop and refer the job to a specialist or to a person with more authority. Read the sections in order: they follow a real job from the first phone call to the handover.

Fault-finding is one of the most dangerous jobs an electrician does. Covers are off, the equipment is not behaving as designed, and the client wants it running again. Plan the safety before you plan the tests.

Nearly every test that finds a fault can be done with the circuit isolated: continuity, resistance, insulation resistance, the diode test and capacitance. Use them first. Seeing the symptom, and the few measurements that can only be made with power on, are done under strict control.

head: Activity
Who does it, and how
rows: Seeing the symptom with the power on
A competent person energises the equipment while you watch from a safe place behind the marked line, with covers on where possible. At the Centre only the instructor or assessor energises anything.
Live measurements (voltage, running current, thermal imaging)
Only a competent, authorised person, and only when the test cannot be done dead
A risk assessment, and a second person present
A meter rated for the job (CAT III or CAT IV), and probes with finger guards and short exposed tips
Insulated tools, barriers, and the PPE the risk assessment sets, such as insulating gloves and an arc-rated face shield
Dead tests
After safe isolation and proving dead. This is where you, as a trainee, do your testing.

flow: Find every source of supply from the drawings and on site
Tell the people affected and agree the shutdown
Switch off at the isolator for the equipment
Lock off with personal padlocks, on a multi-lock hasp for a team
Fit a danger tag
Prove the tester on a proving unit
Test dead between every pair of conductors at the point of work
Prove the tester again
Make stored energy safe: capacitors, drives, batteries and moving parts

blocks.note: At Level 3 you are responsible for the people working with you. Check each junior's lock, tag and dead test yourself before they start. 'I switched it off' is not proof.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Source
Why it is dangerous
What to do
rows: A control supply from somewhere else
Some panels take their control or alarm supply from another board or a UPS. The main isolator is off, but control wiring is still live.
Check the drawings for supplies from outside the panel; some panels mark these wires in orange or with a warning label. Isolate them too, and test every terminal you will touch.
Standby generator with an automatic transfer switch
Switching off the JPS supply can make the generator start and re-energise the panel.
Lock the generator's controls off so it cannot start, as well as isolating.
Solar PV and battery inverters
PV panels make DC whenever there is daylight; batteries keep circuits live in an outage.
Follow the system's shutdown procedure and isolate both the AC and DC sides.
UPS units
The output stays live from the batteries when the input is off.
Shut down as the maker says; treat battery terminals as always live.
Shared or borrowed neutrals
A neutral shared with another circuit can carry that circuit's current while yours is off.
Isolate every circuit that shares the neutral, and test before you disconnect any neutral.

head: Where
The danger
Safe practice
rows: Motor start and run capacitors
Can hold a charge up to the peak of the supply voltage (about 310 V on a 220 V supply) after the supply is off.
Discharge through a suitable resistor or discharge tool, as the maker or instructor shows, then check with a meter.
Power supply smoothing capacitors
A switch-mode supply on 220 V charges its main capacitor to about 310 V DC. Large low-voltage capacitors can give a big spark.
Discharge and measure before touching or testing.
Variable speed drives
The DC bus capacitors stay charged at several hundred volts for minutes after isolation.
Wait at least the time on the drive's label, then measure the DC bus at the terminals the maker gives.
Power factor correction capacitors
Large capacitors at full supply voltage.
Their discharge resistors need time to work: wait the time on the label, then prove dead.
Moving parts
Fans, belts and pumps can keep turning after switch-off, or be turned by air or water flow.
Wait for them to stop; block or brake them where needed.

blocks.note: Never discharge a capacitor by shorting its terminals with a screwdriver. The flash can burn your hands and eyes, and it damages the capacitor and the tool.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: You can carry a static charge of several thousand volts without feeling it, and much less than that can damage a chip or transistor, often without any visible mark, so that it fails later. When you handle boards and components:

ul: Wear an earthed **wrist strap**. Its lead has a built-in resistor (usually 1 MΩ) so that it is safe for you.
Work on an **anti-static mat** connected to the same earth point.
Keep new parts in their anti-static bags until you fit them, and hold boards by their edges.
Work on boards only when they are disconnected from every supply. A wrist strap must not be worn near live mains parts, because it gives your body a path to earth.

blocks.note: A fault means the equipment is not behaving as designed. A welded contact, a shorted button or a wrong connection can start a motor without warning. Keep hands and tools clear of moving parts, and keep guards on until the equipment is isolated.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Changing parts until something works wastes the client's money, leaves the real cause in place and can create new faults. A logical method finds the fault faster and gives you evidence for your report.

flow: Gather information
Confirm the symptom safely
List the likely causes
Plan the tests
Isolate and test in order, recording each reading
Find the fault and its root cause
Repair with the correct parts
Test, and have the system function-tested

head: Ask the client
Why it helps
rows: What exactly happens, and what should happen?
Gives the symptom in their words. Sometimes it is not a fault at all, but a wrong setting or wrong use.
When did it start, and did anything change just before?
A repair, new equipment, an alteration, a storm or a power cut often points straight to the cause.
Does it happen all the time, or only sometimes?
A fault that comes and goes needs a pattern before you can find it.
Under what conditions: heat, rain, heavy load, a time of day?
Heat points to overload or loose joints; rain to water entry; a time of day to timers or other loads switching on.
Has it happened before, and what was done?
A fault that keeps coming back means the root cause was never found.
Was there a smell, a noise, smoke or a trip?
Points to overheating, mechanical failure or a short circuit.

blocks.p: Then read the job history, the maintenance log, the drawings, the maker's manual and the nameplates, and note any fault codes or alarm records. Look for obvious signs: tripped devices, blown fuses, indicator lamps, burn marks, water, corrosion and rodent damage.

May read normal on a meter: a meter's tiny test current hides it. Find it by inspection, tightness checks or thermal imaging

ul: **Easiest and most likely first.** Check the fuse and the overload before you strip a motor.
**Half-split.** In a chain of parts in series, test in the middle. The result tells you which half holds the fault; then split that half, and so on. Each test halves the search.
**Input to output.** Follow the power or signal from the supply towards the load until it stops; or work back from the output.
**Compare with a known-good one.** An identical circuit, panel or board that works gives you the readings to expect.
**Substitute only on evidence.** Swap in a known-good part only when your tests point to it, never as guesswork.

blocks.p: **Half-split example.** A control circuit has 16 links in series and one is open. Test across links 1 to 8: good, so the break is in 9 to 16. Test across 9 to 12: open, so it is in 9 to 12. Test across 9 and 10: open. Test link 9: good, so link 10 is the open one. **Four tests** instead of up to sixteen.

Write every reading on the job sheet as you take it: what you tested, between which points, the instrument and range, the reading with its unit, and the value you expected. The record shows how you found the fault, supports your report and the bill, and gives the next technician values to compare with.

blocks.note: Decide what reading you expect before each test. If the result surprises you, stop and think: either you have found the fault, or the test was wrong.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The **root cause** is the reason the fault happened. If you fix only the symptom, the fault comes back.

Check the function and range before connecting. On the current range it is almost a short circuit: across a supply it can cause an arc flash.

Where it applies
rows: CAT II
Plug-in equipment and outlet circuits
CAT III
Distribution boards, fixed wiring, motors and starters
CAT IV
The origin of the installation: service, meter and incoming supply

blocks.p: Use a meter and leads rated for the highest category and voltage where you will measure. A cheap meter used in a distribution board can explode if a spike hits it.

blocks.h: False readings and how to avoid them

ul: **Ghost voltages.** A digital multimeter has a very high input resistance, so a disconnected conductor running beside live cables can show tens of volts that have almost no power behind them. A two-pole tester, or the meter's low-impedance (LoZ) setting, shows the true result.
**Parallel paths.** Measured in circuit, a part's resistance can read low because other parts are connected across it. Lift one leg, or disconnect one end, and test again.
**Leads not nulled.** Lead resistance is added to every low-resistance reading.
**Wrong function, range or socket.** A flat battery, a blown meter fuse or leads in the current socket can give a zero reading on a live circuit.
**Poor contact.** Corrosion, paint or varnish under the probe tip gives a high reading.
**Temperature.** Copper's resistance rises by about 0.4% for every °C, so a hot winding reads higher than a cold one.

head: Rule
Use
Worked example
rows: Ohm's law: V = I × R, so I = V ÷ R
Coil current, fault current, expected readings
A 24 V DC relay coil of 600 Ω draws 24 ÷ 600 = 0.04 A = 40 mA.
Power: P = V × I
Load current from a rating
A 220 V, 1 100 W load draws 1 100 ÷ 220 = 5 A.
R = V² ÷ P
Expected resistance of an element
A 220 V, 3 000 W element should read about 220 × 220 ÷ 3 000 ≈ 16 Ω.
P = I² × R
Heat in a resistor or a bad joint
A loose joint of 0.1 Ω carrying 30 A makes 30 × 30 × 0.1 = 90 W of heat in one small spot: as much as a soldering iron.
P = V² ÷ R
Power rating of a resistor
100 Ω with 10 V across it dissipates 10 × 10 ÷ 100 = 1 W; fit at least a 2 W resistor.
Voltage drop = I × R
Volt drop on a cable
20 A through a cable of 0.25 Ω (out and back) drops 5 V.
Tolerance
Is a part within its marking?
40 µF ±5% may read from 38 µF to 42 µF.

blocks.p: Read from the end with the bands closest together: first digit, second digit, multiplier, then tolerance (gold ±5%, silver ±10%, brown ±1%). **Example:** red, red, orange, gold = 2, 2, × 1 000 = 22 000 Ω = 22 kΩ ±5%. Small capacitors use a number code in picofarads: 104 = 10 followed by four zeros = 100 000 pF = 100 nF.

head: When it trips
What it points to
How to find it
rows: At once on reset, even with every load unplugged
Short circuit or earth fault in the fixed wiring
Isolate; insulation-test line to neutral, line to earth and neutral to earth; split the circuit at junctions.
At once when one item is switched on or plugged in
A fault in that item or its lead
Test the item and its lead dead.
After running for some time
Overload; a failing motor or bearing; or a loose terminal heating the breaker
Add up the loads or have the current measured; check terminals for heat marks.
The RCD/GFCI trips but the breaker does not
Leakage to earth: water, a leaky element, or many small leakages added together
Insulation tests to earth; split the circuit; a leakage clamp used by a competent person.
The RCD trips when a load is switched on, but the load tests good
A neutral touching earth somewhere after the RCD, or a neutral borrowed from another circuit
Insulation-test neutral to earth; check that each circuit's neutral goes back through its own RCD.
Only in wet weather
Water getting into outdoor fittings, boxes or cables
Inspect outdoor equipment; insulation-test after rain.
During storms, with damage to electronics
Surges from lightning or switching
Check surge protection and earthing.

blocks.note: Do not reset a breaker again and again to 'see what happens'. Each reset onto a short circuit puts a large fault current through the wiring and the breaker. Investigate dead first.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Finding an earth fault with insulation tests

flow: Isolate, lock off and prove dead
Disconnect lamps, LED drivers, electronic equipment and surge protective devices
Test line to earth, neutral to earth and line to neutral at the board
If a reading is low, split the circuit at a junction near its middle
Test each half; the low half holds the fault
Keep halving until you reach the faulty cable, box or fitting
Repair, then retest the whole circuit and reconnect what you removed

ul: For 110/220 V circuits the usual test voltage is **500 V DC**. Current British guidance asks for at least **1 MΩ**; healthy circuits usually read hundreds of megohms.
A circuit that passes the minimum but reads far lower than similar circuits deserves a closer look: it is often getting worse.
Electronic parts can be destroyed by the test voltage, and they make the reading false. Disconnect them, or follow the maker's test instructions.
Warn others before testing. The tester charges the cable: let it discharge through the tester before you touch the conductors.

blocks.p: A loose or corroded joint has extra resistance, and the heat it makes is P = I² × R. At a heavily loaded terminal that can be tens of watts in a small spot. The joint heats, oxidises, gets worse and can start a fire. Signs: discoloured terminals and insulation, a burnt smell, flicker, voltage dropping under load and breakers tripping at normal load because their terminal heats the trip element.

ul: Look for it by inspection, by checking tightness with the circuit isolated, and by thermal imaging under load (by a competent person).
Remake the joint to the maker's tightening torque. Cut back conductors to clean, undamaged copper.
Replace any breaker, terminal block or busbar that has been overheated: its metal may have lost its springiness.
Aluminium conductors need terminals marked for aluminium and a jointing compound, as the maker says.

Electronics fail after storms

blocks.h: Lost neutral on a 110/220 V supply

blocks.p: On a JPS 110/220 V supply each line is about 110 V to neutral and the two lines are 220 V to each other. The shared neutral carries the difference between the currents on the two lines. If that neutral breaks, the 110 V loads on line 1 and line 2 end up **in series across 220 V**, and the 220 V divides between them according to their resistance.

**Example.** The loads on line 1 add up to 20 Ω and those on line 2 to 80 Ω. With the neutral broken, line 1's loads get 220 × 20 ÷ 100 = 44 V and line 2's loads get 220 × 80 ÷ 100 = 176 V. The **lightly loaded side** (higher resistance) gets the high voltage, and its electronics burn out. Each time a load switches on or off, the split changes. The line-to-line reading stays a normal 220 V, which shows that the lines themselves are fine.

ul: Switch off at the main to protect equipment while you trace the neutral.
Check the neutral terminations at the main panel and any sub-panel, splices on the neutral, the meter base and the service drop connection.
With the neutral open, current may try to return through bonding and earthing conductors and metal pipes. Do not disconnect them while the supply is on.

blocks.note: A broken neutral in the service drop, at the meter or anywhere on JPS's side must be repaired by JPS. Report it as an emergency, and keep the main switch off meanwhile.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Faults that come and go are caused by vibration, heat (it works cold and fails hot), moisture, a particular load, or a time of day. Ways to catch them:

ul: Get the pattern from the client: when, how often, what else was happening.
Inspect connections closely; flex cables and move connectors while watching a continuity reading, with the circuit isolated.
Have a competent person log the voltage or current over a day, or use a meter's minimum and maximum memory.
On boards, the instructor may gently heat or cool parts to make the fault appear.
If you cannot find it, say so honestly in the report, record what you tested, and tell the client what to note if it happens again.

sections.title: Motor control circuits, sensors and drives

head: Drawing
Shows
Use it to
rows: Schematic (ladder) diagram
How the circuit works, in rungs between two supply rails, with contacts drawn in their rest state
Follow the logic step by step and plan your tests.
Wiring (connection) diagram
Actual terminals, wire numbers and where each wire goes
Find where to put your probes.
Panel layout drawing
Where each part sits in the panel
Find the parts.
Block diagram
The main sections and how signals flow between them
Decide which section holds the fault.

ul: Contacts are drawn in their **rest** state: not pressed, not energised. A normally open (NO) contact closes when operated; a normally closed (NC) contact opens.
A coil and its contacts carry the same label, such as K1 or KM1, so you can find every contact the coil works.

Common terminal numbers: contactor coil **A1–A2**; auxiliary NO contacts 13–14 and 43–44; auxiliary NC contacts 21–22 and 31–32; overload trip contact **95–96** (NC) and alarm contact 97–98 (NO); timer contacts 15–16 (NC) and 15–18 (NO).
Wire numbers on the drawing match ferrule numbers on the wires.

blocks.h: How a direct-on-line (DOL) starter's control circuit works

flow: Control fuse
STOP button (NC) and any emergency stops (NC)
START button (NO), with the hold-in contact 13–14 in parallel
Overload contact 95–96 (NC)
Contactor coil A1–A2
Back to the other side of the control supply

blocks.p: Pressing START energises the coil. The contactor closes its main contacts to the motor and its auxiliary **hold-in contact**, which bypasses START so the motor keeps running when START is released. Pressing STOP, an emergency stop or an overload trip breaks the coil circuit and the contactor drops out. After a power cut the contactor also drops out and the motor does not restart by itself: this **no-volt protection** is a safety feature.

blocks.h: What the competent person sees with power on

blocks.p: In a live series control circuit, a closed, healthy contact has almost **0 V** across it, and an open contact has nearly the **full control voltage** across it. Measuring from one side of the control supply along the circuit, the competent person finds the point where the voltage stops. You will not take these readings as a trainee, but you must be able to read and use them.

head: Device
How it works
Typical faults
rows: Float switch
A float tilts or slides to open or close a contact at a water level
Contact burnt open, float stuck, cable damaged
Pressure switch
Opens or closes at set pressures
Blocked pipe to the switch, wrong setting, burnt contacts
Limit switch
A lever or plunger is moved by the machine
Bent lever, loose mounting, water in the body
Proximity sensor
Senses metal (inductive) or an object (photoelectric) without touch; usually 24 V DC with an indicator LED
Wrong distance, dirty lens, damaged cable, wrong wiring (PNP or NPN type)
Photo-eye safety beam (gates, doors)
Stops or reverses the motor when the beam is broken
Misaligned, dirty, or sun shining into the receiver
PLC inputs and outputs
A small controller reads inputs and switches outputs by its program
Use the input and output LEDs as a half-split point: is the signal reaching the PLC, and is the PLC switching its output?

blocks.p: A VSD rectifies the supply to DC, stores it on large **DC bus capacitors**, and switches it to make a variable-frequency supply for the motor. When it trips, it shows a fault code. Record the code and the conditions before resetting, then look the code up in the maker's manual.

head: Fault code type
Common causes
rows: Overcurrent
Acceleration time too short for the load, a jammed or heavy load, a motor or cable fault
Overvoltage
Deceleration time too short, so the load drives the motor and pumps energy back into the drive
Undervoltage
Supply dips or a lost phase
Overtemperature
Blocked fan or filters, a hot room or enclosure
Earth fault
Damaged insulation on the motor cable or in the motor

ul: Keep a written or saved copy of the drive's settings. A reset to factory values loses the motor data and the ramp times.
Wait the time on the drive's label after isolation, then measure the DC bus before touching anything inside.
**Never insulation-test through a drive.** Disconnect the motor cable at the drive's output terminals and test the cable and motor from there.

head: Motor
How it starts or runs
Common faults
rows: Single-phase capacitor-start (compressors, pumps, workshop machines)
A start winding and start capacitor give starting torque; a centrifugal switch or start relay cuts them out at about three-quarters of full speed

Hums but will not start with a free shaft: start capacitor, starting switch or start winding. Capacitor failing again and again: the switch is sticking closed, because a start capacitor is made for only a few seconds' use at each start.
Permanent split capacitor (fans, air-conditioning fan motors)
A run capacitor stays in circuit all the time
Runs slowly, runs hot or will not start: weak or failed run capacitor, often from heat in outdoor units.
Three-phase induction
Three phases make a rotating field
Single-phasing (one phase lost): hums and will not start, or runs on and overheats. Wrong rotation: swap any two supply lines, with the motor isolated.

blocks.note: The overload is set to the motor's full-load current. Never turn it up, bridge it or fit a larger one to stop it tripping: find out why the motor is drawing too much current.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Never link out an emergency stop, guard switch, interlock or overload 'just to get the line running'. These protect people. A system with a safety device bypassed must not be put back into use.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Many control panels, alarm panels and gate controllers contain a simple linear power supply. Knowing what each stage does tells you what each fault looks like.

flow: Fuse and transformer: step 220 V AC down, for example to 18 V AC
Bridge rectifier (four diodes): turn AC into pulsing DC
Smoothing capacitor: fill the gaps between pulses
Regulator: give a steady output, such as 12 V or 5 V
Load: relays, logic, sensors and indicator LEDs

blocks.p: **The numbers.** An AC voltage's peak is about 1.41 times its RMS (meter) value. An 18 V AC secondary peaks at about 18 × 1.41 ≈ 25 V. Two diodes conduct at a time, each dropping about 0.6–0.7 V, so the capacitor charges to about 24 V on light load. A regulator needs its input a few volts above its output. With a full-wave bridge on a 50 Hz supply, the capacitor is topped up 100 times a second, so the ripple is at **100 Hz**; a half-wave rectifier tops it up only 50 times a second, so the ripple is larger.

head: Faulty part
Symptom
Dead test (board disconnected, capacitor discharged)
rows: Primary fuse blown
Nothing works
Continuity. Find out why it blew, such as a shorted diode or capacitor, before you replace it.
Transformer winding open
No AC on the secondary
Winding resistance reads OL.
One bridge diode open
Works as a half-wave rectifier: lower DC, much larger ripple, resets and buzzing relays
Diode test: OL in both directions.
One bridge diode shorted
Fuse blows
Diode test: near 0 V in both directions.
Smoothing capacitor dried out or open
Large ripple, hum, random resets
Capacitance or ESR meter; look for a bulged top or leaking.
Regulator failed
Input correct, output 0 V or equal to the input
Replace; the competent person confirms input and output voltages.
Overload on the output
Regulator very hot, output voltage falls
Check the load for a short.

blocks.p: Most modern equipment uses switch-mode supplies: smaller and lighter, but more complex. On 220 V their main capacitor charges to about 310 V DC and can stay charged after unplugging. Common faults are dried-out or bulged electrolytic capacitors, a shorted switching transistor that blows the fuse, and dry joints. Repairs on the mains side are for trained people only; often the right repair is to replace the whole module with the same type.

head: Component
How to identify it
Test
Typical failure
rows: Resistor
Colour bands or a printed code; larger body for higher power
Ohms range, with one leg lifted if in doubt
Burnt, open, or drifted high in value. Find out why it overheated.
Electrolytic capacitor
Value in µF, voltage rating; a stripe marks the negative lead
Capacitance or ESR meter after discharge
Bulged, leaking, dried out (low value, high ESR)
Film or ceramic capacitor
Number code in pF, such as 104 = 100 nF
Capacitance range
Shorted, open or cracked
Diode
The band marks the cathode
Diode test: about 0.6–0.7 V one way, OL the other
Shorted (near 0 both ways) or open (OL both ways)
LED
Longer lead is the anode; flat edge marks the cathode
Diode test; it may glow faintly. Forward voltage about 1.8–3.3 V
Open, or dim from heat damage
Zener diode
Like a diode, marked with its zener voltage
Diode test forward; its zener voltage needs a powered test
Shorted or open
Bipolar transistor
Three leads: base, collector, emitter (check the data sheet)
Diode test: base to collector and base to emitter each behave like a diode
Collector to emitter shorted
Voltage regulator
Three leads: input, common, output (check the data sheet)
Powered test by a competent person
Output dead or equal to the input
Relay
Coil terminals and contact terminals on the case
Coil resistance; contact continuity when operated
Open coil, burnt or welded contacts
Board fuse
Marked with current and speed
Continuity
Blown: find the cause

blocks.p: A transistor often switches a relay coil. When the coil is switched off, its magnetic field collapses and makes a high voltage spike. A **diode fitted across the coil** (reverse-biased, with its band to the positive side) gives that spike a safe path. If the diode is missing, open or fitted the wrong way, the transistor keeps failing; fitted the wrong way, it also shorts the supply.

blocks.note: Testing in circuit: parts connected in parallel change your reading. A diode that reads 0.3 V both ways in circuit may be fine, with a low resistance beside it. If a reading looks wrong, lift one leg and test again.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Item
Notes
rows: Temperature-controlled soldering iron
Tip temperature is typically about 320–370 °C for through-hole work; follow the solder maker's figure. Keep the tip clean and tinned.
Solder
Tin-lead solder melts at about 183–190 °C. Lead-free solder melts at about 217–221 °C and needs a hotter tip and a little more time.
Flux
Cleans the metal so the solder wets it. Most solder wire has flux in its core.
Desoldering pump and braid (wick)
Remove old solder without overheating the pad.
Heat-sink clip
Clamped on a lead to protect a heat-sensitive part.
Magnifier, side cutters, tweezers
Inspect joints and trim leads.
Fume extractor
Flux fumes can cause asthma.

flow: Photograph the board and note the orientation of diodes, capacitors and chips
Disconnect the board, discharge capacitors, put on the wrist strap
Heat each joint and remove the solder with the pump or braid
Lift the part out without forcing it, so the plated holes are not torn
Clean the pads
Fit the new part the right way round and bend the leads slightly to hold it
Heat pad and lead together for two or three seconds and feed solder into the joint, not onto the iron
Remove the solder, then the iron; do not move the part as it cools
Trim the leads and inspect each joint with the magnifier
Clean off flux if the maker requires it

head: Joint
Looks like
Cause and cure
rows: Good joint
Smooth, concave fillet that wets both pad and lead; the lead's outline shows. Tin-lead is shiny; lead-free is a little duller and satin but the same shape
Dry (cold) joint
Dull, grainy, cracked, or a ball sitting on the pad without wetting it
Not hot enough, dirty pad or lead, or moved while cooling. Remove the solder, clean and resolder.
Solder bridge
Solder joining two pads or tracks that should be separate
Too much solder or a dragged iron. Remove the excess with braid.
Too much solder
A large blob that hides whether the joint has wetted
Remove some with braid and inspect again.
Too little solder
Hole not filled; pad partly bare
Add solder with fresh flux.
Lifted pad or track
Copper pad or track peeled off the board
Overheating or force. Repair only as the instructor shows, for example with a wire link.

blocks.p: Surface-mount parts are tiny and need a fine tip or hot-air tool and tweezers. Many surface-mount repairs are done by replacing the board or module.

blocks.note: Use fume extraction and wear safety glasses: clipped leads and solder can fly. Put the iron back in its stand every time, and switch it off when you finish. Solder may contain lead: wash your hands before eating or drinking, and do not eat at the bench.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Think about
Questions to ask
rows: Cost
Does the repair, parts and labour together, come close to the price of a new item?
Parts and time
Can the parts be bought in Jamaica, or must they be imported? How long will the client be without the system, and what does that cost them?
Age and history
Is the item old or worn? Has it failed before?
Safety and standards
Will a repaired item still be safe and meet the current requirements?
Energy use
Would a new item, such as an LED fitting or an efficient motor, cut the client's electricity bill?
Warranty
Is it under the maker's warranty? Opening it may cancel the warranty.

blocks.p: Give the client the options with prices in J$ and the time each will take. Let the client decide, and record the decision.

head: Part
Must match
rows: Fuse
Current rating, speed (quick-blow or time-delay), breaking capacity, voltage rating and size
Circuit breaker
Current rating, trip type or curve, breaking capacity, number of poles
Contactor
Coil voltage and AC or DC; current or kW rating for the duty (AC-3 for motors); auxiliary contacts; mounting
Overload relay
A setting range that includes the motor's full-load current
Capacitor
Capacitance; the same or a higher voltage rating; start or run type; temperature rating; polarity for electrolytics
Resistor
Value, tolerance and power rating
Semiconductor or regulator
The same part number, or an equivalent confirmed from the data sheet: voltage, current, pin-out and package
Cable or wire
Size, type and temperature rating

blocks.note: A quick-blow fuse in place of a time-delay fuse blows on every motor start. A larger fuse, breaker or overload lets cables and windings overheat without tripping. A lower voltage capacitor can burst. The wrong part is never 'close enough'.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Check your work: terminals tight, no bare copper, covers and guards back, no tools or offcuts left inside
Dead tests: protective conductor continuity, insulation resistance and polarity, as they apply
Compare the results with the expected values and record them
Remove locks in the agreed order; a competent person energises
Function test: controls, interlocks, emergency stops, direction of rotation, running current against the nameplate
Watch it run under normal load to be sure the fault does not return
Clean up and hand back

head: Section
What to write
Why
rows: Job details
Client, address, date, equipment and its number, who did the work
Identifies the job.
Reported problem
What the client said
Shows why you were called.
Tests and readings
Each test, the points, the reading and its unit
Shows how you found the fault; a record for next time.
Fault and root cause
What failed and why
Helps the client avoid a repeat.
Work done and parts
Parts fitted with their ratings
Supports the bill and any warranty.
Tests after repair
Dead and function test results
Shows the system is safe.
Recommendations
Other defects found, worn parts, improvements, with an estimate in J$
Lets the client plan and protects you.
Time and signatures
Hours, your signature, the client's acknowledgement
Completes the record.

ul: **Agree the shutdown** with the client before you start: when it starts, how long it lasts, who must be told, and what must be protected, such as freezer stock, production or computer data.
Have likely spare parts on hand before the shutdown, so the system is not off longer than needed.
Give each team member a clear role, such as tester, recorder and checker, and match tasks to their skill.
Check juniors' isolation, method and readings. Correct mistakes straight away and explain why.
Explain the fault and the repair to the client in plain words, and show them the failed part where it helps.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can gather information about a fault from the client, the records, the drawings and the manuals.
I can find every source of supply and stored energy in a system and make it safe before testing.
I can explain why live testing is kept for competent, authorised people, and read the results they give me.
I can protect electronic parts from static.
I can plan a logical test order, use the half-split method and record my readings.
I can choose the right instrument, range and CAT rating, and spot ghost voltages and other false readings.
I can use Ohm's law and the power formulas to work out expected readings.
I can tell an overload, a short circuit and an earth fault apart from when and how a device trips.
I can locate an earth fault by insulation testing and splitting the circuit.
I can explain a lost neutral on a 110/220 V supply and what to do about it.
I can read a ladder schematic and find faults in a DOL starter by dead tests.
I can find faults in sensors, float switches and capacitor-start motors.
I can work safely on a variable speed drive and test its motor without damaging it.
I can test the parts of a DC power supply and identify an open or shorted diode, a failed capacitor and a failed regulator.
I can desolder and solder a component and judge the joint.
I can find the root cause of a fault rather than treating the symptom.
I can choose replacement parts with the correct ratings and advise on repair or replacement.
I can test after repair and arrange a function test by a competent person.
I can write a clear fault report and explain it to the client.
I can lead a small team on a fault-finding job and check their work.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: The JPS supply to homes and most businesses
About 0.6–0.7 V
Forward reading of a silicon diode on the diode test
Peak of an AC voltage from its meter (RMS) reading
About 310 V DC
Charge on a capacitor fed from 220 V AC
100 Hz / 50 Hz
Ripple frequency of full-wave / half-wave rectifiers on a 50 Hz supply
500 V DC, at least 1 MΩ
Insulation test voltage and current British minimum for 110/220 V circuits
6 to 8 × full-load current
Typical direct-on-line starting current of a motor
About 0.4% per °C
Rise in copper's resistance with temperature
1 MΩ
Safety resistor in an anti-static wrist strap lead
Melting range of tin-lead / lead-free solder
About 320–370 °C
Typical soldering iron tip temperature
30 mA / about 5 mA
Trip level of an RCD / a GFCI for protecting people

terms: Bridge rectifier
Four diodes that turn AC into pulsing DC, using both halves of each cycle.
CAT rating
A meter's measurement category (II, III or IV), showing where it can be used safely.
Dry (cold) joint
A poor solder joint that is dull, grainy or cracked and does not make reliable contact.
Earth fault
A fault in which current flows from a line conductor to earthed metal or the ground.
Electrostatic discharge (ESD)
A static spark that can damage electronic parts without being felt.
ESR
Equivalent series resistance: rises as an electrolytic capacitor dries out.
Ghost voltage
A voltage shown by a high-impedance meter on a disconnected conductor, coupled from nearby live cables, with almost no power behind it.
Half-split method
Testing in the middle of a chain of parts, so that each test halves the area left to search.
High-resistance joint
A loose or corroded connection that heats up under load.
Hold-in contact
The auxiliary contact that keeps a contactor energised after START is released; also called the holding or latching contact.
Intermittent fault
A fault that comes and goes.
Ladder (schematic) diagram
A drawing that shows how a control circuit works, in rungs between two supply rails.
Lost neutral
A broken shared neutral on a 110/220 V supply, which gives high voltage on one side and low voltage on the other.
No-volt protection
The way a contactor drops out after a power cut, so the motor does not restart by itself.
Overload
More current than a circuit or motor is designed to carry; also the relay that protects a motor against it.
Ripple
The AC wobble left on a DC supply after rectifying and smoothing.
Root cause
The underlying reason for a fault, which must be fixed so the fault does not return.
Short circuit
A fault in which line touches neutral or another line, so a very large current flows.
Single-phasing
Loss of one phase of a three-phase supply to a motor.
Smoothing capacitor
The large capacitor that fills the gaps between rectified pulses.
Solder bridge
Solder that wrongly joins two pads or tracks.
Variable speed drive (VSD)
Equipment that controls a motor's speed by changing the frequency of its supply.
Voltage regulator
A component that keeps a DC output steady, such as 12 V or 5 V.

c1.title: A packing-line conveyor in Hayes
c1.text: Kerry-Ann, a Level 3 trainee, leads two Level 2 trainees on a breakdown at a citrus packing house in Hayes, Clarendon. A conveyor's direct-on-line starter has a 220/24 V control transformer, a STOP button, a latching emergency stop at the far end of the line, a START button, an overload relay and a contactor with a 24 V AC coil. When the maintenance supervisor energises the panel and presses START, the 'control on' lamp is lit but nothing happens: no click. With the panel isolated, locked off and proved dead, the team reads: control fuse 0.1 Ω; STOP closed; START closes when pressed; overload contact 95–96 closed; coil 41 Ω, the same as a new coil in stores.

c2.title: A gate controller in Stony Hill
c2.text: Mr Wright's maintenance team looks after the electric gate at a townhouse complex in Stony Hill, St Andrew. The gate controller's logic board has its own power supply: a transformer with an 18 V AC secondary, a bridge rectifier of four diodes, a 2200 µF 35 V electrolytic smoothing capacitor and a 12 V regulator. Since a thunderstorm last week the controller resets at random and its relay buzzes. With the board disconnected and the capacitor discharged, one bridge diode reads OL in both directions on the diode test range; the other three read about 0.6 V one way and OL the other.

c3.title: Bright and dim rooms at a Port Antonio guest house
c3.text: Miss Bryan owns a six-room guest house in Port Antonio, Portland, supplied by JPS at 110/220 V. This morning the lamps in rooms 1 to 3, on line 1, are very bright and a television there has failed, while the lamps in rooms 4 to 6, on line 2, are dim and their fans run slowly. The pattern changes when the kitchen kettle or microwave is switched on. The team's competent person measures at the main panel: line 1 to neutral 158 V, line 2 to neutral 62 V, line 1 to line 2 220 V.

c4.title: A kitchen extract drive at a Runaway Bay hotel
c4.text: The kitchen extract fan at a hotel in Runaway Bay, St Ann, is a 5.5 kW three-phase motor run by a variable speed drive (VSD) in a panel on the roof. Last week a contractor reset the drive to its factory settings after a power cut. Since then the drive trips with an 'overcurrent' code each time the fan speeds up, although the fan and motor turn freely by hand when isolated. The drive's label says 'Wait 10 minutes after disconnecting power'. Ricardo, a Level 3 technician, leads the job.

c5.title: An ice plant compressor in Yallahs
c5.text: An ice plant in Yallahs, St Thomas, has a belt-driven compressor with a single-phase 220 V capacitor-start motor, fitted with a start capacitor and a centrifugal switch. This morning it hummed and would not start, and its breaker tripped after a few seconds. With the motor isolated, the shaft turns freely, the start capacitor's case is bulged and it reads 0 µF. The job history shows the start capacitor was replaced twice in the last four months. The capacitor is marked 189–227 µF, 250 V AC; the run winding reads 1.8 Ω and the start winding 4.1 Ω.

questions.q: Which part of the control circuit should the team test next?
o: The motor windings, at the starter's output terminals
The contactor's main contacts, with the low-resistance ohmmeter
The emergency stop and its cable out along the line
The panel's incoming supply fuses, on the main side
questions.why: The lamp shows the control supply is present, and every part of the coil circuit tested so far is good. The only part of that circuit not yet tested is the emergency stop and its long cable. The main contacts, the motor and the incoming fuses cannot stop the contactor from clicking.

questions.q: The emergency stop reads open even when it is reset. A trainee suggests a wire link across it so the line can run until a new one arrives. What should Kerry-Ann decide?
o: Allow the link for one shift if someone stands by the panel
Allow the link, as the STOP button at the panel still works
Move the stop into the panel, so the long cable is not needed
Refuse the link and keep the line off until the stop works
questions.why: An emergency stop lets someone at the far end of the line stop it when a person is caught. Linking it out removes that protection, and the STOP button at the panel may be too far away. Have it repaired or replaced, and tell the supervisor and the client why the line stays off.

questions.q: Stores has no 24 V contactor, only one of the same size with a 220 V AC coil. What would happen if it were fitted in this panel unchanged?
o: Its coil would get far too little voltage to pull in
It would pull in harder, so its contacts would last longer
Its coil would burn out at once from too much current
It would work normally, as only the main contacts matter
questions.why: A coil must match the control supply. With 24 V on a 220 V coil it gets about a ninth of its rated voltage, so it will not pull in, or will chatter. The opposite mistake, 220 V on a 24 V coil, burns the coil out. Match the coil voltage, the current rating and the duty.

questions.q: Suppose the open circuit had been somewhere among 16 links in series in this coil circuit. Using the half-split method, about how many continuity tests would find the open link?
o: About 8
About 4
About 16
About 2
questions.why: Each test halves the part left to search: 16 links, then 8, then 4, then 2, then 1, which is four tests. Testing link by link from one end could take up to sixteen.

questions.q: What does the reading on the odd diode tell the team?
o: It is open, so only half of each cycle is rectified
It is fine, since a good diode blocks current both ways
It has failed short, and will soon blow the board's fuse
It is fitted backwards, so the output polarity is reversed
questions.why: A good silicon diode reads about 0.6–0.7 V one way and OL the other. OL both ways means it is open. A bridge with one open diode works as a half-wave rectifier: the capacitor is topped up only 50 times a second instead of 100, so the ripple grows and the output dips, which explains the resets and the buzzing relay. A shorted diode reads near zero both ways.

questions.q: If the smoothing capacitor is replaced as well, which of these is suitable?
o: 2200 µF 16 V, fitted either way round, as the value matches
1000 µF 35 V, as a smaller one charges up more quickly
4700 µF 10 V, as a bigger value always smooths better
2200 µF 50 V, fitted with its stripe to the negative side
questions.why: The capacitor charges to about the peak of 18 V AC (18 × 1.41 ≈ 25 V) less about 1.4 V for the two conducting diodes: about 24 V. A 16 V or 10 V capacitor would fail, and may burst. Fit the same capacitance with the same or a higher voltage rating, with the stripe (negative lead) on the negative side: an electrolytic fitted backwards overheats.

questions.q: The diode failed just after a thunderstorm. What should the repair report recommend to stop it happening again?
o: A larger fuse on the primary side of the small transformer
Surge protection for the controller, with its earthing checked
A larger smoothing capacitor, to keep the ripple small in future
No action, since diodes simply wear out after a few years
questions.why: Lightning and switching surges come in on the supply and on the long cables to the gate motor, sensors and keypad. The likely root cause is a surge, so recommend a surge protective device and a check of the earthing. A bigger fuse or capacitor would not stop a surge, and diodes do not normally wear out.

questions.q: After a new diode is fitted, one of its joints looks dull and grainy, with a crack round the lead. What should be done?
o: Add more solder on top, so that the joint looks shiny again
Leave it, as lead-free solder always gives a dull joint
Remove the solder, clean the pad and make the joint again
Put a drop of glue on the lead so that it cannot move
questions.why: Dull, grainy and cracked is a dry joint: the solder has not wetted pad and lead, often because the joint was not hot enough or moved as it cooled. Lead-free joints are a little duller than tin-lead ones, but a good one is still smooth and wets both pad and lead. Adding solder on top only hides the fault.

questions.q: Which reading shows that both of JPS's lines are still reaching the panel normally?
o: Line 1 to neutral, which reads above 110 V
Line 1 to line 2, which still reads 220 V
Line 2 to neutral, which reads below 110 V
None of them, since all three readings are wrong
questions.why: The line-to-line reading does not use the neutral at all, and it is a normal 220 V, so both lines are present. The faulty part is the shared neutral: with it broken, the two 110 V halves are in series across 220 V and share it unequally.

questions.q: Why do rooms 1 to 3, on line 1, get the high voltage?
o: Line 1 has the lighter load, so it takes more of the 220 V
Line 1 has the heavier load, so it draws more voltage to it
JPS has raised line 1 to make up for the low voltage on line 2
The breakers on line 1 are larger, so more voltage gets through
questions.why: With the neutral broken, the loads on the two lines are in series across 220 V and the voltage divides in proportion to their resistance. A lighter load has a higher resistance, so it takes the bigger share, here 158 V. Electronics on that side burn out, and the split changes each time a load switches on or off.

questions.q: What should be done first, while the fault is traced?
o: Unplug the television and leave everything else on till evening
Fit a larger main breaker so that the voltages even out again
Disconnect the main bonding conductor to stop stray current
Switch off at the main until the neutral is found
questions.why: Every minute with the neutral open can damage more equipment, so switch off. Then trace the neutral: the panel's neutral bar and terminations, the meter base and the service drop; a break on JPS's side is reported to JPS. Never disconnect bonding or earthing now: with the neutral open they may be carrying current and can give a shock.

questions.q: Given what changed last week, what is the most likely cause of the trips?
o: The speed-up time is now too short for the heavy fan
The fan blades are now too light for the drive's power
The motor's bearings have failed and seized up solid
The drive's display has begun showing the wrong code
questions.why: A large fan has a lot of inertia. Factory settings often give a short acceleration ramp, so the drive must push a high current to speed the fan up, and it trips on overcurrent. Compare the settings with the commissioning record and the manual, set the ramp and motor data again, and keep a copy of the settings. The fan turns freely, so the bearings are not seized.

questions.q: Ricardo wants to insulation-test the motor and its cable. How should this be done?
o: Test at the drive's input terminals, so the whole system is covered
Leave the drive connected, but raise the test voltage to 1000 V
Read the insulation value from the drive's display while it runs
Disconnect the motor leads at the drive's output, then test
questions.why: An insulation tester's high DC voltage applied through the drive can destroy its electronics, and the drive makes the reading meaningless. After isolating and waiting, disconnect the motor cable at the drive's output terminals and test the cable and motor from there, then reconnect it to the maker's torque.

questions.q: The drive has been isolated, locked off and tagged for 3 minutes. Before anyone touches its DC terminals, what must happen?
o: Nothing more, as the supply was proved dead at its isolator
Short the DC terminals with a screwdriver to drain them
Switch off the drive's keypad, which drains the capacitors
Wait the label's 10 minutes, then prove the DC bus dead
questions.why: The DC bus capacitors stay charged at several hundred volts after the supply is removed; their discharge resistors need the time on the label. Then measure the DC bus with a suitable meter at the terminals the maker gives. Shorting them with a screwdriver causes a dangerous flash.

questions.q: What is the most likely root cause of the repeated capacitor failures?
o: The run winding is open, so the start capacitor does all the work
The capacitors are too large in µF for this motor's start winding
The centrifugal switch is not opening, so the capacitor stays in
The breaker is rated too low and damages the capacitor as it trips
questions.why: A start capacitor is made for a few seconds' use at each start. If the centrifugal switch sticks closed, the capacitor stays in circuit, overheats, bulges and fails, and the start winding overheats too. Check the switch's contacts and mechanism. The run winding reads 1.8 Ω, so it is not open.

questions.q: Which replacement capacitor should be fitted?
o: A start capacitor marked 88–108 µF, 250 V AC
A start capacitor marked 189–227 µF, 330 V AC
A run capacitor marked 200 µF, 250 V AC, as it lasts longer
A start capacitor marked 189–227 µF, 125 V AC
questions.why: Fit the same capacitance range, of the start type, with the same or a higher AC voltage rating. A 330 V AC rating is fine on a 250 V AC duty. A smaller value gives poor starting torque, a 125 V rating would fail at once, and a run capacitor is the wrong type for this duty.

questions.q: Which entry for the fault report will help the next technician most?
o: Motor would not start; repaired it and it now runs well again, all good
Cap read 0 µF and bulged; switch stuck closed; cap and switch renewed
Third capacitor this year, so the client should buy a new motor soon
Capacitor looked bad so it was replaced; the switch seemed fine
questions.why: A useful entry gives the evidence (the readings), the fault, its root cause and the parts fitted, so the next technician knows what happened and what to check. The readings after the repair also go on the report. Vague notes and unsupported advice do not help.

questions.q: A replacement 47 Ω resistor will have 9 V across it. Which power rating should it have, at least?
o: 0.25 W, as small resistors suit low voltages
At least 5 W, since it will dissipate about 423 W
At least 2 W, since it will dissipate about 1.7 W
0.5 W, since it will dissipate about 0.19 W
questions.why: Power = V² ÷ R = 9 × 9 ÷ 47 ≈ 1.7 W. A resistor run close to its rating gets very hot, so choose a higher rating: at least 2 W here. If the old one burnt, find out why before fitting the new one.

questions.q: A disconnected line conductor in an isolated circuit shows 38 V AC to earth on a digital multimeter, but nothing on a two-pole tester proved before and after. What is the most likely explanation?
o: A ghost voltage picked up from live cables beside it
The circuit is fed from a generator that the team missed
The multimeter's battery is flat, so its readings are random
The two-pole tester has reached the end of its working life
questions.why: A digital multimeter has a very high input resistance, so it can show a voltage coupled from nearby live cables with almost no power behind it. A two-pole tester, or a meter's low-impedance (LoZ) setting, loads the conductor and shows the true result. The tester was proved before and after, so its result stands.

questions.q: A thermal camera survey of a loaded board shows one breaker terminal at 78 °C, while similar breakers carrying similar current are at 38 °C. What should the report recommend?
o: Fit a small fan inside the board to cool that terminal down
Swap that breaker for one with a higher current rating
Isolate, remake the joint, replace any heat damage, rescan
Scan the board again next year to see if it gets hotter
questions.why: A terminal much hotter than similar ones carrying the same current points to a loose or high-resistance connection, which gets worse and can start a fire. Plan a shutdown, isolate, remake the connection to the maker's torque, replace any heat-damaged breaker or conductor, and scan again under load.
